content:
A meme circulating on social media sets two pictures side by side. In the first, a Muslim smiles at the Christian diagram of the Trinity and says "3 gods". In the next panels he paints his own face as a clown while copies labelled Hafs, Warsh, Qalun and some twenty other names pile up beside him, and he insists there is still "1 Quran".

The meme makes an argument, and it deserves an answer. The names on the covers are real, the editions are printed, and some of them differ in words as well as in sounds. This article aims to provide context to those names, insha'Allah, in seven answers: what the names are, what they share, how Muslims recorded them, what the differences look like, what they change, and why the comparison with the Trinity fails.

The Quran itself frames the question: "Do they not reflect upon the Quran? If it had been from other than God, they would have found within it much contradiction" (4:82).[1]

Hafs, Warsh, Qalun, al-Bazzi, Qunbul and the rest are the names of men. Each was a transmitter (rawi) who learned the recitation of the Quran from one of the great teachers of the early centuries, and passed it on with a chain of teachers that runs back to the Companions.[2]

There are ten such teachers, called the readers (qurra'), and each has two principal transmitters. Hafs and Shu'ba transmit from 'Asim of Kufa; Qalun and Warsh transmit from Nafi' of Medina. The twenty names on the meme's covers are those twenty transmissions.[2]

The transmission of Hafs is the one most Muslims recite today, and it is the basis of the 1924 Cairo printing used across most of the Muslim world. The transmission of Warsh is the one most widely recited in North and West Africa, where printings in Warsh are the ordinary Quran of the mosque and the home.[3]

So a printed copy "of Hafs" is the Quran as recited in the transmission of Hafs from 'Asim. Each of these printings contains the same 114 surahs, in the same order, with the same text. The schools of verse-counting divide some passages differently, so a Warsh printing numbers some verses differently from a Hafs printing, while the words counted are the same.[2]

When the caliph 'Uthman sent standard copies of the Quran to the provinces, around 650, the copies were written in the Arabic script of the time, which marked the consonants and left most of the vowels unwritten. That written skeleton is called the rasm, and we set out the history of the copies in our article on Uthman's copies.

The scholars of recitation accepted a reading only if it met three conditions, as Makki ibn Abi Talib set them out and Ibn al-Jazari adopted them: a sound and well-known chain of transmission, agreement with the rules of Arabic, and agreement with the writing of at least one of the 'Uthmanic copies.[4]

A reading that failed the third condition was set aside, however good its chain. The readings on the meme's covers are therefore so many ways of voicing a single written text, all of them within its letters.[4]

The variety goes back to the Prophet's own lifetime, and the most trusted collection records it. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab heard Hisham ibn Hakim recite Surat al-Furqan "in several different ways" from the way 'Umar had been taught. He brought Hisham to the Prophet, who approved both recitations and said that the Quran was revealed in seven modes (ahruf).[5]

The scholars then catalogued what was recited. Ibn Mujahid of Baghdad, who died in 324 AH (936), fixed seven readers in his Kitab al-Sab'a. Ibn al-Jazari, who died in 833 AH (1429), set out ten, with their transmitters and chains, in al-Nashr fi al-Qira'at al-'Ashr.[6]

The commentators did the same. Al-Tabari, discussing the opening surah of the Quran, notes that the readers differed over one word and refers the reader to his separate Kitab al-Qira'at, where he had already set out who read what and why he preferred one reading.

The meme presents the readings as something Muslims hide. The record is the reverse: the Muslim scholars named every reader, every transmitter and every difference, and wrote the books from which the meme's list was drawn.

Most differences between the readings are differences of vowels and of the dots that tell one consonant from another. Christopher Melchert's study of a sample of the ten readings found these to be the commonest kinds, with changes to the written skeleton itself much rarer.[7]

Some differences change a word. In 2:85 Hafs reads "you do" where Warsh reads "they do"; in 19:19 the angel says to Mary "that I may give you" in Hafs and "that He may give you" in Warsh; in 43:19 Hafs speaks of the angels "who are servants of the Most Merciful" and Warsh of those "who are with the Most Merciful".[8]

Al-Tabari, writing in the tenth century, gives a classic case in the opening surah. Some readers recite 1:4 as maliki yawm al-din, "King of the Day of Judgement", and others as maliki with a long first vowel, "Owner of the Day of Judgement". He explains both: one is from mulk, kingship, and the other from milk, ownership.[9]

The written skeleton itself differs in only a handful of places. One is 42:30, where Hafs reads "then it is because of what your hands have earned" and Warsh reads the same words without "then". The regional copies of 'Uthman differed in a small number of such letters, and every canonical reading follows one of them.[8]

The paired readings say two true things about one subject. God is both the King and the Owner of the Day of Judgement, and the Quran calls Him both elsewhere: "Sovereign of mankind" (114:2) and "Owner of sovereignty" (3:26). The angels are both God's servants and near to Him, and the Quran says both (21:26; 7:206).[10]

The changes of person, "you" and "they", "I" and "He", follow a habit the Quran shows in every reading. Its speech turns from one person to another within a single passage, a device the Arab rhetoricians called iltifat; we set it out in our article on why the Quran switches between He, We and I.[10]

A few readings carry more weight. In 12:90 one transmission has Joseph's brothers say "You are Joseph" and another "Are you Joseph?"; in 5:6 the readings of the word for "feet" were debated by the jurists in the law of ablution.

These are the hardest cases, and the jurists and commentators discussed them in the open. None of them touches a doctrine of faith.[8][11]

Al-Tabari's treatment of 5:6 shows how those discussions were held. He records Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others reading "your feet" in the accusative and explaining that "the command returns to washing", and he weighs the other reading beside it. The disagreement was argued in commentaries that anyone could read.[11]

The meme's comparison rests on treating two different claims as one. "One Quran in several recorded readings" is a claim about a text and how it is recited, and it can be checked: every reading is printed, every difference is listed, and every one sits within the same written skeleton.[4]

"One God in three persons" is a claim about the nature of God, and it is the doctrine in dispute. The Quran answers it directly: "Do not say: Three. Desist; it is better for you. God is only one God" (4:171), and "Say: He is God, One" (112:1).[1]

The readings of the Quran have never been the subject of that disagreement. Hafs, Warsh and every other reading agree that God is one, that Jesus is His servant and messenger, and that He neither begets nor is begotten.[1]

If the meme wants a test of "one book", the Bible is a better case for it. Christians do not agree on how many books their Bible contains: the Council of Trent fixed a canon of seventy-three books for the Catholic Church, Protestant Bibles have sixty-six, and the Eastern and Oriental churches keep longer lists that differ among themselves.[12]

Those are differences in what the book is, beyond how its words are read. Within the New Testament, the two oldest complete codices end Mark at 16:8 and leave out the story of the woman taken in adultery, and the clause on the three heavenly witnesses in 1 John 5:7 entered the printed Greek only in the sixteenth century. We set out the evidence in our articles on the oldest Bible codices and the Comma Johanneum.

None of this is a reason for mockery on either side of the argument. It is a reason to compare like with like: the Quran's readings with the Bible's manuscripts and canons, judged by what each tradition recorded about its own text.

The bottom line

Hafs, Warsh, Qalun and the other names on the meme are twenty transmitters of ten recognised readings, each tied by a chain to the Companions and each bound to the written text of the 'Uthmanic copies. The Prophet approved recitation in more than one mode, and Muslim scholars recorded every difference in books that are still printed.

Most differences are vowels and dots; a few change a word, and the changed words say two things the Quran affirms elsewhere. The readings are one Quran recited in recorded ways, and that claim can be checked.

The Trinity is a claim about God, and the Quran answers it in four verses (112:1-4). God knows best.

Notes

  1. Quran 4:82; 4:171; 112:1–4.
  2. On the ten readers and their transmitters, see Ibn al-Jazari, al-Nashr fi al-Qira'at al-'Ashr, vol. 1; IslamWeb, Fatwa No. 91213, "The ten ways of reciting the Quran", 27 February 2006, https://www.islamweb.net/en/fatwa/91213/the-ten-ways-of-reciting-the-quran.
  3. IslamWeb, Fatwa No. 118960, "Popularity of the recitation of Hafs from Aasim", 9 March 2009, https://www.islamweb.net/en/fatwa/118960/popularity-of-the-recitation-of-hafs-from-aasim; IslamWeb, Fatwa No. 91555, "The Quranic recitations published in the world", 27 March 2006, https://www.islamweb.net/en/fatwa/91555/the-quranic-recitations-published-in-the-world.
  4. Ahmad Ali al-Imam, Variant Readings of the Qur'an: A Critical Study of Their Historical and Linguistic Origins (London and Washington: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 2006), chapter 6, on the conditions for accepted readings as set out by Makki ibn Abi Talib and Ibn al-Jazari.
  5. Sahih al-Bukhari 4992, Book of the Virtues of the Quran, report of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab; compare Sahih al-Bukhari 2419.
  6. Ibn al-Jazari, al-Nashr fi al-Qira'at al-'Ashr, vol. 1, p. 81 (Shamela text), on Ibn Mujahid's Kitab al-Sab'a.
  7. Christopher Melchert, "The Relation of the Ten Readings to One Another", Journal of Qur'anic Studies 10.2 (2008), pp. 73–87.
  8. On the Hafs and Warsh readings of 2:85, 19:19 and 43:19, and on 12:90, see the verse-by-verse comparison of the ten readings and their twenty transmissions at nquran.com, https://www.nquran.com; the same examples are tabulated in the article "Qira'at" in the English Wikipedia.
  9. Al-Tabari, Jami al-Bayan (Mecca: Dar al-Tarbiya wa-l-Turath, n.d.; vols. 1–16 ed. Mahmud Muhammad Shakir), vol. 1, pp. 147–151, on Quran 1:4, https://shamela.ws/book/43/158.
  10. Quran 114:2; 3:26; 21:26; 7:206.
  11. Quran 12:90; 5:6, with al-Tabari, Jami al-Bayan, vol. 10, pp. 52–64, on 5:6, the readings of "your feet" and the reports for each, from report 11447, https://shamela.ws/book/43/5320.
  12. On the Catholic canon, the Council of Trent, fourth session (1546), Decree concerning the canonical Scriptures; on the other canons, Bruce M. Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1987), and the canon lists of the Eastern and Oriental churches.
